title: Interfaces and Cables
summary: How devices are connected: copper UTP cabling, RJ-45 connectors, pin layouts, straight-through vs crossover, fiber optics, and the Ethernet standards that define them.

sections.title: Interfaces, ports, and why standards matter

content.body:
An **interface** (also called a **port**) is where a device connects to the network. Switches typically have many interfaces (24 or more) to connect end hosts.

An **RJ-45** port (RJ = Registered Jack) is the familiar wired-network socket on PCs and switches, and the RJ-45 connector is the plug at the end of a copper Ethernet cable.

**Why standards exist:** two people who speak different languages can't talk. Network protocols serve that same role for devices — they are an agreed-upon system of communicating. Without industry standards for connector shape, speeds, and protocols (both physical, like cables, and logical, like IP), devices from different vendors couldn't connect.

A **bit** is a 0 or a 1 — everything in computing is ultimately a series of bits. On a copper cable, variations in the electrical signal are interpreted by the receiver as 0s and 1s. **8 bits = 1 byte.**

**Network speed is measured in bits per second** (kilobits, megabits, gigabits per second), because data travels along a wire one bit at a time — never one byte at a time.

Data stored on a hard drive, however, is measured in **bytes**. A gigabyte is 8 times larger than a gigabit.

1 kilobit = 1,000 bits · 1 megabit = 1 million bits · 1 gigabit = 1 billion bits · 1 terabit = 1 trillion bits.

Ethernet copper cables are **UTP** — **Unshielded Twisted Pair**. 'Unshielded' means the wires have no metallic shield (making them vulnerable to electrical interference); the **twisted pairs** help protect against **electromagnetic interference (EMI)**.

A UTP cable has **4 pairs** (8 wires total), and the RJ-45 connector has 8 pins. However, not every standard uses all 8 wires:

- **10BASE-T / 100BASE-T**: use 2 pairs — pins **1-2** and **3-6**
- **1000BASE-T / 10GBASE-T**: use all 4 pairs — pins **1-2**, **3-6**, **4-5**, **7-8**

A PC or router **transmits on pins 1-2** (Tx) and **receives on pins 3-6** (Rx). A switch is the opposite: it **receives on pins 1-2** and **transmits on pins 3-6**. Because each device uses separate wire pairs to send and receive, **full-duplex** transmission is possible — both devices send data at the same time with no collisions.

steps.narration: A straight-through cable connects pin 1 to pin 1, pin 2 to pin 2, pin 3 to pin 3, etc. PC transmits on pins 1-2, and the switch receives on pins 1-2 — they complement each other.
The switch transmits on pins 3-6, and the PC receives on pins 3-6. Full-duplex communication works with no problem.

Two routers both transmit on pins 1-2 and receive on pins 3-6. With a straight-through cable, the left router transmits on pins 1-2, but the right router isn't prepared to receive there — communication fails.
A crossover cable reverses the pairs: pin 1 connects to pin 3, pin 2 to pin 6. Now the transmit pins on one side connect to the receive pins on the other.
With the pairs crossed over, both routers can send and receive data normally.

content.body:
Most modern networking devices include **Auto MDI-X**, which automatically detects which pins the neighbor is transmitting on and adjusts its own Tx/Rx pins to match.

With Auto MDI-X, connecting two switches (or two routers, or two PCs) with a *straight-through* cable works fine — the devices self-correct. Unless you're working with quite old equipment, you don't need to worry about straight-through vs crossover cables in practice, but the concept is fair game for the exam.

sections.title: Fiber optic cables and SFP transceivers

content.body:
Many switches and routers have **SFP** (**small form-factor pluggable**) ports. You insert an SFP transceiver into the port, and connect a **fiber optic cable** to it. Instead of electrical signals over copper, fiber sends **light over glass fibers**.

A fiber cable has **two connectors on each end** — one to transmit and one to receive — because fiber uses separate physical cables for each direction.

**Fiber cable structure**, from center to outer layer:
1. **Core** — the glass fiber that light travels down
2. **Cladding** — reflects light back into the core
3. **Buffer** — protects the fiber from breaking
4. **Outer jacket**

modes.label: Multimode
modes.description: Wider core, multiple light modes enter at various angles, LED transmitters. Cheaper; shorter distances than single-mode.

modes.label: Single-mode
modes.description: Narrower core, light enters at a single angle, laser transmitters. More expensive; longest distances.

rows: More expensive SFP (single-mode more than multimode)

content.body: When picking a cable for a distance question: **under 100 m on the same floor** → UTP. **150 m between buildings** → multimode fiber (supports it, cheaper than single-mode). **3 km between offices** → single-mode fiber (multimode doesn't reach). Remember the cost trade-off: UTP is cheapest but shortest, single-mode is priciest but longest, multimode sits in between.

questions.question: You connect two old routers together with a UTP cable, however data is not successfully sent and received between them. What could be the problem?
questions.explanation: Both routers transmit on pins 1-2, so a crossover cable is needed to connect the transmit pins on one side to the receive pins (3-6) on the other. Modern Auto MDI-X would fix this, but the old routers may not support it. A crossover cable would likely fix the issue.

options.label: A
options.text: They are connected with a straight-through cable

options.label: B
options.text: They are connected with a crossover cable

options.label: C
options.text: They are operating in Auto MDI-X mode

questions.question: Your company wants to connect switches in two separate buildings that are about 150 meters apart, keeping costs down if possible. What kind of cable should they use?
questions.explanation: UTP keeps costs down but doesn't support distances over 100 meters. Single-mode fiber supports much longer distances but is more expensive than multimode. Multimode fiber supports over 150 meters and is cheaper than single-mode — the best answer.

questions.question: Your company wants to connect two offices that are about 3 kilometers apart, keeping costs down if possible. Which kind of cable should they use?
questions.explanation: UTP doesn't support 3 km. Multimode fiber is cheaper than single-mode but also doesn't support 3 km. Many single-mode fiber standards support much longer than 3 km, so although it's more expensive, it is necessary here.

questions.question: A switch has Auto MDI-X enabled on its network interfaces. What would happen if you connect it to an identical switch with a straight-through cable?
questions.explanation: The ports are Auto MDI-X enabled, so they will operate normally regardless of whether a straight-through or crossover cable is used. They would not operate at a reduced speed, and they would not be unable to communicate.

options.label: B
options.text: They would operate at a reduced speed

options.label: C
options.text: They would be unable to communicate

questions.question: Your company needs to connect many end hosts to a switch in a wiring cabinet on the same office floor as the hosts. What kind of cable should they use?
questions.explanation: Most hosts can't connect via fiber, and most switches don't have enough SFP interfaces for many hosts. UTP is the standard for wired connections to switches — hosts have an RJ-45 port on their NIC and switches have many RJ-45 ports.
